newsitem.title: BOSNIA: After poll, Bosnia mulls how to make system work.
newsitem.headline: After poll, Bosnia mulls how to make system work.

text.p: The Western architects of Bosnia's first post-war elections were set on Thursday to start looking at ways of making the fledgling state's new democratic institutions work following strong showings by nationalists.

After Moslem president Alija Izetbegovic claimed victory in the race to head the three-man presidency, international peace coordinator Carl Bildt said he expected the former rival communities would cooperate to overcome the bitterness of wartime.

"Now that we have the preliminary results for the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, we can discuss the tasks for 1997 and the consolidation of peace," Bildt said after meeting the German and British defence ministers in Sarajevo.
Izetbegovic claimed a narrow win in the contest to head the new collective leadership over his Serb rival, hardline separatist Momcilo Krajisnik of the Serb Democratic Party (SDS).
The Croatian Democratic Party's representative Kresimir Zubak will join the other two nationalist leaders to form the multi-ethnic executive.
Under the Dayton peace accord, the presidency must reach a consensus on every decision although Izetbegovic will represent Bosnia abroad.
While Izetbegovic won his job on a campaign for national unity, Krajisnik's faction argued for Serb independence.
Hardliners in the HDZ Croat movement also harbour ambitions of splitting their territory away from Bosnia and grafting it to neighbouring Croatia.

Final results for Bosnia's other administrative units including its joint federal parliament were expected to be released later on Thursday. But early figures gave the three major nationalist parties unassailable leads.
With wartime leaders returned to power clutching popular mandates, diplomats fear the new democratic institutions will be struggling to function.

The international community's next major task -- and the presidency's first test -- will be to convene the presidency and its parliament. This is a difficult goal given that no venue or even a date has been agreed upon.
Western diplomats say they expect Izetbegovic, Krajisnik and Zubak to cooperate -- at least initially -- if only to stave off threats of indefinite U.N. sanctions.
But privately diplomats warn that the Dayton-enshrined commitment to consensus could lead to political gridlock if any one party decides it is unwilling to compromise on decision-making.
If it was unclear how the joint democratic institutions would function, many Bosnians, irrespective of ethnic loyalty, appeared willing to accept the outcome and live under the new system.
Damir, a 23-year-old Moslem student celebrating Izetbegovic's victory in Sarajevo said the Moslem president was "the lesser evil" among the nationalist leaders.
"I hope he will keep his promise about multi-this and multi-that," Damir told Reuters.
On the other side of the former front lines, local Serbs said they were resigned to living under a Moslem president.
Zoran Stevic, a refugee living in the strategic town of Brcko, said he would have preferred Krajisnik to have won, but he would accept the result.
"I don't think there will be any problems," he said. "The people have had enough of war. In the end, we will have our own president of the Bosnian Serb Republic, Biljana Plavsic."

Another refugee in Brcko, 19-year-old Natasa who used to live in Sarajevo agreed: "Everything will go back to normal in time, and maybe it won't be important who is (federation) president, because everyone will have his own (entity) president anyway."
